title: To Build a Fire
author: Jack London (retold)
summary: 氷点下50度を下回るユーコンの雪原を、一人の男と一匹の犬が歩いていきます。経験者の忠告を軽く見た男を待つものは。ジャック・ロンドンの代表作。

source.note: Retold and shortened from Jack London’s “To Build a Fire” (1908, public domain).

paragraphs: Day had broken cold and gray, extremely cold and gray, when the man turned aside from the main Yukon trail and climbed the high earth bank to a little-traveled path that led east through the thick spruce forest. It was nine o’clock. There was no sun, not even a hint of sun, though there was not a cloud in the sky. It was a clear day, and yet there seemed to be an invisible shadow over the face of things. That was because the sun was absent. It had been days since he had seen the sun, and he knew that a few more days must pass before it would rise, briefly, above the southern horizon.

To the north and south, as far as his eye could see, lay unbroken white. The Yukon River lay hidden under three feet of ice, and on top of the ice lay as many feet of snow. Along the middle ran a thin dark line: the trail that led south five hundred miles to the sea, and north to Dawson and beyond.

But all this — the mysterious, far-reaching line, the absence of sun, the tremendous cold, and the strangeness of it all — made no impression on the man. He was new to the country. This was his first winter. The trouble with him was that he had no imagination. He was quick and alert in the things of life, but only in the things, and not in their meanings. Fifty degrees below zero meant eighty-odd degrees of frost. That fact impressed him as being cold and uncomfortable, and that was all. It did not lead him to think about his weakness as a creature of temperature, or about man’s weakness in general, able to live only within narrow limits of heat and cold. Fifty degrees below zero was something to be guarded against by the use of gloves, ear flaps, warm boots and thick socks. It was nothing more.

As he turned to go on, he spat. There was a sharp, explosive crackle that startled him. He spat again. And again, in the air, before it could fall to the snow, the spit crackled. He knew that at fifty below, spit crackled on the snow, but this spit had crackled in the air. It was colder than fifty below. How much colder, he did not know. But the temperature did not matter. He was going to the old claim on the left fork of Henderson Creek, where the boys already were. He would arrive by six o’clock. A bit after dark, it was true, but the boys would be there, a fire would be going, and a hot supper would be ready.

At the man’s heels trotted a dog, a big native husky, gray-coated and not noticeably different from its brother, the wild wolf. The animal was depressed by the tremendous cold. It knew that it was no time for traveling. Its instinct told it a truer tale than was told to the man by the man’s judgment. In reality, it was not merely colder than fifty below; it was colder than sixty below, than seventy below. It was seventy-five below zero. The dog knew nothing of thermometers, but it had its instinct. It felt a vague but menacing fear that made it follow closely at the man’s heels, and that made it question every unusual movement of the man, as if expecting him to go into camp or to look for shelter somewhere and build a fire. The dog had learned fire, and it wanted fire.

The man’s red beard and mustache were frozen solid. His warm, moist breath came out of his mouth and immediately turned to ice. Tobacco juice he spat froze too, so that a long brown icicle grew down from his chin. If he fell, it would shatter like glass. But he did not mind. He had seen it before.

He walked on, along the frozen creek. He was careful where he stepped. He knew that there were springs under the snow that never froze, even in the coldest weather. Water from these springs lay under the snow, sometimes with a thin skin of ice over it, waiting. Once, when he suspected such a spot, he forced the dog to go in front. The dog went unwillingly. Suddenly it broke through, and its feet and legs came up wet. Almost at once the water on them turned to ice. The dog quickly licked the ice off its legs, then dropped down in the snow and began to bite out the ice that had formed between its toes. This was a matter of instinct. To leave the ice would mean sore feet. The man took off his right glove and helped tear out the ice. He did not leave his fingers bare for more than a minute, and he was astonished at how quickly they went numb.

At twelve o’clock, he stopped to eat lunch. He took off his glove, and before he could get the biscuits from inside his shirt, his fingers were numb. He had to beat his hand against his leg until the feeling returned. He realized that he had forgotten to build a fire to thaw himself first. He laughed at his foolishness. He also remembered the old-timer on Sulphur Creek, who had told him about the cold. Now he was beginning to understand. He built a fire, warmed himself, ate his lunch and smoked a pipe. The dog lay near the fire, close enough for warmth and far enough not to be burned.

When the man had finished, he filled his pipe again, pulled on his gloves, tied the ear flaps of his cap firmly, and continued up the creek. The dog was disappointed and looked back longingly toward the fire.
It happened at a place where there were no signs. The snow looked solid. The man broke through. It was not deep. He wet himself halfway to the knees before he scrambled out to firm ground.

He was angry, and he cursed his luck aloud. He had hoped to get to the camp by six o’clock, and this would delay him an hour, for he would have to build a fire and dry his boots and socks. At this low temperature, that was absolutely necessary. He knew that much. He turned aside to the bank and climbed it. Under some small spruce trees there was a pile of dry wood left by the spring floods. He gathered small sticks and dry grass and built a fire. He worked carefully, aware of his danger. Gradually, as the flame grew stronger, he added bigger sticks.

The old-timer on Sulphur Creek had told him that no man should travel alone in the Klondike after fifty below. Well, here he was. He had had the accident; he was alone; and he had saved himself. Those old-timers were rather womanish, he thought. All a man had to do was keep his head, and he was all right. Any man who was a man could travel alone.
His feet were now ice. To untie his boots, he had to struggle with the frozen laces, his fingers almost useless. He reached for his knife.

But before he could cut the laces, it happened. It was his own fault, or rather his mistake. He should not have built the fire under the spruce tree. He should have built it in the open. Each time he had pulled a twig from the bushes, he had shaken the tree slightly. High up in the tree, one branch was heavy with snow. It fell onto the branch below, which tipped and spilled its load onto the branches beneath it. The snow grew like an avalanche, and it fell without warning upon the man and the fire, and the fire was out. Where it had burned was a mound of fresh snow.

The man was shocked. It was as though he had just heard his own sentence of death. For a moment he sat and stared at the spot where the fire had been. Then he grew very calm. Perhaps the old-timer on Sulphur Creek was right. If he had only had a trail partner, he would be in no danger now. The partner could have built the fire. Well, it was up to him to build the fire again, and this second time there must be no failure.

He made a new foundation for a fire, this time in the open, where no tree could put it out. He gathered dry grass and tiny twigs. But his fingers would not obey him. He could not feel what he was holding. He watched them, to see whether they were holding something.

At last he got out his matches. But his fingers were so stiff that he dropped the whole bunch in the snow. He tried to pick them up, but could not. He pulled off his glove with his teeth and beat his bare hand against his leg. Then, with both hands, he scooped up the bunch of matches, along with much snow. He held them between his two numb hands and, after several attempts, managed to scratch them all at once against his leg. Seventy matches flared into flame together. He held the burning bunch to the dry grass. The smell of his own burning flesh reached him, but he could not feel it. At last a small flame caught the grass. He fed it twigs with the greatest care. But the fire was weak, and his hands were shaking. A piece of green moss fell on the tiny flame. He tried to poke it away, but he scattered the burning grass and twigs, and they went out in thin streams of smoke. The fire provider had failed.

He looked at the dog, sitting across the ruins of the fire, its eyes eager and wondering. A wild idea came to him. He remembered the tale of a man caught in a blizzard who killed a steer and crawled inside the body, and so was saved. He would kill the dog and bury his hands in the warm body until the feeling came back. Then he could build another fire. He called to the dog, but there was a strange note of fear in his voice that frightened the animal. It had never heard the man speak like that before. It would not come close. When at last it came near enough, the man reached out to grab it. But his hands could not hold. He could not draw his knife. He could not even close his fingers. The dog broke away and stood at a distance, watching him with its ears sharply forward.

The man looked down at his hands. They hung at the ends of his arms like weights. A certain fear of death came to him. This was no longer a matter of losing fingers or toes. It was a matter of life and death. He panicked. He turned and ran up the creek along the old trail. The dog followed. He ran blindly, with no purpose, with a fear he had never known before. As he ran, he slowly began to feel better. Perhaps if he ran on, his feet would thaw out. Perhaps he would even reach the camp and the boys. But he did not have the endurance. Several times he stumbled, and at last he fell. When he tried to rise, he failed.

He sat up in the snow and thought about meeting death with dignity. The idea of it was that he had been making a fool of himself, running around like a chicken with its head cut off. Well, he was bound to freeze anyway, and he might as well take it decently. With this new peace of mind came the first faint feelings of drowsiness. A good idea, he thought, to sleep off to death. It was like taking an anesthetic. Freezing was not as bad as people thought. There were many worse ways to die.

He imagined the boys finding his body the next day. Suddenly he found himself with them, coming along the trail and looking for himself. And still with them, he came around a turn in the trail and found himself lying in the snow. He did not belong with himself any more. He was out of himself, standing with the boys and looking at himself in the snow. It certainly was cold, he thought. When he got back to the States, he could tell the folks what real cold was. He drifted on from this to a vision of the old-timer on Sulphur Creek. He could see him quite clearly, warm and comfortable, smoking a pipe.
“You were right, old man; you were right,” the man mumbled to the old-timer of Sulphur Creek.

Then the man drifted into what seemed to him the most comfortable and satisfying sleep he had ever known. The dog sat facing him and waiting. The brief day drew to a close in a long, slow twilight. There were no signs of a fire being made. Besides, never in the dog’s experience had it known a man to sit like that in the snow and make no fire. As the twilight drew on, its eager longing for the fire mastered it. It whined softly, then lifted its feet and whined louder, expecting to be scolded by the man. But the man remained silent. Later, the dog howled loudly. And still later it crept close to the man and caught the scent of death. This made the animal draw back. A little longer it waited, howling under the stars that leaped and danced and shone brightly in the cold sky. Then it turned and trotted up the trail in the direction of the camp it knew, where there were other food providers and fire providers.
